I found the paper you're looking for! Here are the key details:

**Title:** "Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally Can be More Effective than Scaling Parameters for Reasoning"

**Key Findings:**

By optimally scaling test-time compute, the researchers found they can outperform much larger models in a FLOPs-matched evaluation.

The paper explores how much an LLM can improve its performance on challenging prompts when allowed to use a fixed amount of inference-time compute, with implications for the future of LLM pretraining and how to tradeoff inference-time and pre-training compute.

The research analyzes two primary mechanisms to scale test-time computation: (1) searching against dense, process-based verifier reward models (PRMs); and (2) updating the model's distribution over a response adaptively, given the prompt at test time.

The researchers propose a "compute-optimal" scaling strategy that allocates test-time compute per prompt in an adaptive manner, improving the efficiency of test-time compute scaling for math reasoning problems by more than 4x compared to a best-of-N baseline.

In a FLOPs-matched evaluation, test-time compute can be used to outperform a 14x larger model on problems where a smaller base model attains somewhat non-trivial success rates.

The paper was posted in October 2024 and has been accepted for presentation at ICLR 2025.

I found the paper you're looking for! Here's what I found about it:

## Paper Summary

Test-time scaling (TTS) has proven effective in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Verification plays a key role in TTS, simultaneously influencing (1) reasoning performance and (2) compute efficiency, due to the quality and computational cost of verification.

The paper challenges the conventional paradigms of verification, and makes the first attempt toward systematically investigating the impact of verification granularity—that is, how frequently the verifier is invoked during generation, beyond verifying only the final output or individual generation steps.

## Key Contribution

The authors introduce Variable Granularity Search (VG-Search), a unified algorithm that generalizes beam search and Best-of-N sampling via a tunable granularity parameter g. Extensive experiments with VG-Search under varying compute budgets, generator-verifier configurations, and task attributes reveal that dynamically selecting g can improve the compute efficiency and scaling behavior.

**Paper Details:**
- **arXiv ID:** 2505.11730
- **Authors:** Hao Mark Chen and 5 other authors
- **Status:** Accepted at NeurIPS 2025
- **Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11730

- arXiv ID: 2502.14382

**What the Paper Proposes:**

S* is the first hybrid test-time scaling framework that substantially improves the coverage and selection accuracy of generated code. S* extends the existing parallel scaling paradigm with sequential scaling to push performance boundaries. It further leverages a novel selection mechanism that adaptively generates distinguishing inputs for pairwise comparison, combined with execution-grounded information to robustly identify correct solutions.

**Key Results:**

S* consistently improves performance across model families and sizes, enabling a 3B model to outperform GPT-4o-mini. S* enables non-reasoning models to surpass reasoning models - GPT-4o-mini with S* outperforms o1-preview by 3.7% on LiveCodeBench.

"Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents" was authored by Chunqiu Steven Xia and 3 other authors. The paper was initially submitted on July 1, 2024, with a revised version on October 29, 2024.

The paper questions whether complex autonomous software agents are necessary and proposes Agentless as an agentless approach to automatically solve software development problems.

## SWE-bench Verified and Chowdhury

Neil Chowdhury was one of the lead authors on SWE-bench Verified, along with James Aung, Chan Jun Shern, Oliver Jaffe, Dane Sherburn, and others.

SWE-bench Verified is a subset of the original test set from SWE-bench, consisting of 500 samples verified to be non-problematic by human annotators. It is a human-validated subset of SWE-bench that more reliably evaluates AI models' ability to solve real-world software issues.

On SWE-bench Verified, GPT-4o resolves 33.2% of samples, with the best performing open-source scaffold, Agentless, doubling its previous score of 16% on SWE-bench.

The paper introducing SWE-bench Verified was released by OpenAI in collaboration with the original SWE-bench authors and has become an important benchmark for evaluating AI coding systems and large language models on real-world software engineering tasks.

**Overview:**
SWE-bench is an evaluation framework consisting of 2,294 software engineering problems drawn from real GitHub issues and corresponding pull requests across 12 popular Python repositories.

**Task Description:**
Given a codebase along with a description of an issue to be resolved, a language model is tasked with editing the codebase to address the issue.

**Complexity:**
Resolving issues in SWE-bench frequently requires understanding and coordinating changes across multiple functions, classes, and even files simultaneously, calling for models to interact with execution environments, process extremely long contexts and perform complex reasoning that goes far beyond traditional code generation.

**Performance Results:**
State-of-the-art proprietary models and fine-tuned models can resolve only the simplest issues, with the best-performing model, Claude 2, able to solve a mere 1.96% of the issues.

## SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering

SWE-agent is a system that facilitates language model agents to autonomously use computers to solve software engineering tasks.

**Key Details:**
- **arXiv ID:** 2405.15793
- **Authors:** John Yang and 6 other authors (including Carlos E. Jimenez, Alexander Wettig, Kilian Lieret, Shunyu Yao, Karthik Narasimhan, and Ofir Press)
- **Published:** Originally submitted May 6, 2024; latest version November 11, 2024
- **Venue:** Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024)

**Main Contribution:**
The paper introduces the concept of the agent-computer interface (ACI) and demonstrates how careful ACI design can substantially improve language model agent performance without modifying the underlying LM's weights. The authors build, evaluate, and open-source SWE-agent, a system that provides language models an ACI for solving real-world software engineering tasks.

**Performance:**
Using GPT-4 Turbo as a base language model, SWE-agent solves 12.47% of the 2,294 SWE-bench test tasks, substantially outperforming the previous best resolve rate of 3.8% by a non-interactive, retrieval-augmented system.

**Resources:**
- Full paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793
- GitHub repository: https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent
